title: What makes a serial killer?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore what makes a serial killer: the origin of the term (coined by Robert Ressler in the mid-1970s), how serial killers differ from mass murderers and spree killers, the FBI three-victim definition and cooling-off period, famous cases (H. H. Holmes, Jeffrey Dahmer, Ted Bundy, Son of Sam, BTK, Green River killer, Gary Ridgeway, Ed Gein, Robert Pickton, Aileen Wuornos, Fred Shipman, Pedro Alonso Lopez), motive-based typologies (visionary, missionary, lust, thrill, power-seeking), organized vs. disorganized killers, the McDonald triad, insanity defense and antisocial personality disorder, sociological explanations, brain abnormality studies, profiling, modus operandi and signatures, and the Peter Woodcock weekend-pass case. The episode also includes banter about Josh quitting smoking, show announcements (New York events, T-shirt contest, Co-Ed donation drive) and a listener mail top-ten list.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the serial killer topic, Josh announces he has quit smoking, and they introduce the episode and a goodie-bag note for new listeners.

segments.title: Origin of the term serial killer
segments.summary: Chuck explains that Robert Ressler coined the term serial killer in the mid-1970s, a former FBI officer, who was inspired by movie serials; earlier terms like mass murder are mentioned. Hosts note that serial killers usually lack an obvious motive.

segments.title: Mass murderers, spree killers, and serial killers distinguished
segments.summary: Hosts define mass murderers (four or more victims at about the same time and place) and spree killers, then give the FBI definition of a serial killer (three or more victims with a cooling-off period between killings), using Jeffrey Dahmer's gaps as an example.

segments.title: How many serial killers and early cases
segments.summary: Hosts estimate about 400 serial killers in the US over the past century, with most since 1900, and name H. H. Holmes and his Chicago hotel near the World's Fair as an early case. They discuss false confessions and inflated victim counts in cases like Henry Lee Lucas and Wayne Williams.

segments.title: Classifying serial killers by motive
segments.summary: Hosts describe the Holmes and DeBurger typology based on motive: act-focused killers (visionary and missionary) and process-focused killers (lust, thrill and gain, and power-seeking). Examples include Son of Sam, the Green River killer, and John Wayne Gacy.

segments.title: Organized versus disorganized killers
segments.summary: Hosts contrast organized killers, who are often educated, follow the news, and may taunt police, with disorganized killers, who tend to live alone and have nighttime habits. They mention Dexter as organized and Robert Pickton as disorganized.

segments.title: McDonald triad and childhood warning signs
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the McDonald triad of childhood behaviors (bedwetting, arson, cruelty to animals) and Chuck admits he had some of these traits as a kid. They also note Jeffrey Dahmer's troubled childhood with abandonment and neglect.

segments.title: Neglect, abuse and Dahmer's behavior
segments.summary: Hosts describe research finding that serial killers often experienced childhood neglect and abuse, and mention a study showing neglected rats developing sociopathic traits. They recount Dahmer's behavior, including his attempts to create a companion zombie with drain cleaner and his cannibalism.

segments.title: Insanity defense and antisocial personality disorder
segments.summary: Hosts read the US insanity defense standard and explain that serial killers rarely meet it. They discuss Ed Gein as one of the few who got an insanity plea, and describe antisocial personality disorder and its seven diagnostic criteria, which Josh jokingly applies to himself.

segments.title: Sociological explanations of serial killing
segments.summary: Hosts present a sociological view, attributed to a sociologist they interviewed, that serial killing is a product of society rather than mental illness. The argument links social change since 1950 and the marginalization of prostitutes to rising targeting of prostitutes. They also cite a study finding brain abnormalities in some confessed killers.

segments.title: Profiling and modus operandi
segments.summary: Hosts explain how investigators build profiles from signatures and modus operandi, which evolve as killers learn from mistakes. They discuss how the van was a common lure vehicle and that Ted Bundy's profile was largely accurate, and then describe how the BTK killer was caught after sending a floppy disk with metadata.

segments.title: Notable cases: Woodcock, Shipman, Garavito
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Peter Woodcock, who killed on a weekend pass from a Canadian psychiatric hospital, and list other prolific killers: Harold Shipman (doctor who killed patients), Pedro Alonso Lopez-style cases are not named, and Luis Alfredo Garavito in Colombia who was released early.

segments.title: Show announcements and sponsor reads
segments.summary: Hosts announce New York events at the Knitting Factory and a trivia night, promote a T-shirt contest, and encourage a five-dollar text donation to Co-Ed for textbook and computer centers.

segments.title: Listener mail: top ten reasons to hate the show
segments.summary: A listener named Noah sends a humorous top-ten list of reasons to hate the show, including misused pronouns, the theme music, and Jerry being rarely mentioned. The hosts respond and ask for serial killer stories.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and remind listeners to send serial killer stories to the show email, and mention the sponsor line.
